material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

notes.text:
# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
At the dossier contact conditions, X0 should give the largest single-contact organic recovery and best nominal product/impurity selectivity among the four extractants. A complete process retaining the organic phase after X0 extraction should therefore outperform X1–X3 unless the dossier is misindexed or reaction-medium effects dominate. Test: compare otherwise matched batches; a clearly inferior X0 final recovery/purity would weaken this claim.

## H2 [tentative]
Reaction conversion/selectivity likely depends categorically on catalyst and solvent and nonlinearly on temperature/time. I will screen categories before local refinement; anonymous indices imply no ordinal trend.

## Decision rule
Recommend only a completed batch with measured final purity >=0.80, prioritizing recovery among qualifying batches. Differences near stated assay noise will be treated as unresolved unless replicated.

# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [partially supported]
X0 remains the working extractant because it has the strongest nominal single-contact partition/selectivity prior, but no matched experimental extractant comparison has yet isolated this effect. The claim remains conditional on the dossier indexing.

## H2 [supported in screened scope]
For 360 K, 1800 s reactions at 0.003 mol catalyst and 0.04 L solvent, C1/S2 is the best screened category pair. The pre-workup HPLC response for C1/S2 (event runner-operation-0091: yield 0.147, selectivity 0.681) exceeded C1 with S0, S1, or S3 and C2/C3 with S0 (events runner-operation-0023, -0074, -0109, -0040, -0057). These are single runs with categorical confounding outside the C1 solvent subset.

## H3 [supported but confounded]
Cooling to about 298 K after quench before extraction likely preserves target during workup. The first cooled C1/S2 batch achieved final purity 0.901 and recovery 0.0353 (runner-operation-0104), higher recovery than prior uncooled batches; solvent and reaction category differences confound the comparison. Test by retaining C1/S2 and refining reaction/workup.

## Decision
Use C1/S2 for remaining optimization. Qualifying leader is batch 6; it changes if another completed batch has purity >=0.80 and materially higher recovery.

# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [working prior; not isolated experimentally]
X0 remained the selected extractant because its dossier gave the strongest nominal single-contact product partition/selectivity. No matched X0–X3 workup comparison was completed, so any causal claim about extractant identity remains unresolved.

## H2 [supported in screened scope]
C1/S2 was the best screened catalyst/solvent category pair at 360 K and 1800 s (pre-workup HPLC runner-operation-0091 versus -0023, -0040, -0057, -0074, and -0109). Anonymous indices are treated strictly as categories.

## H3 [supported in this process sequence]
With C1/S2 and post-quench cooling, increasing reaction temperature from 380 to 440 K at 1800 s increased pre-workup target response and final recovery while retaining qualifying purity: batch 8 (runner-operation-0140, recovery 0.0519), batch 9 (-0158, 0.0904), batch 10 (-0176, 0.0991), batch 11 (-0194, 0.1103). The monotonic numerical trend is not extrapolated beyond 440 K, and each level is unreplicated.

## H4 [supported, with paired-condition evidence limited by run variability]
At 440 K, replacing two 0.03 L washes with one 0.04 L wash increased final recovery from 0.1103 in batch 11 to 0.1524 in batch 12 while purity decreased from 0.867 to 0.846 (runner-operation-0194 versus -0211). Both remain above the 0.80 purity constraint; the recovery gain is several assay standard deviations, although only one run per wash scheme was performed.

## Final decision
Recommend completed batch 12: 0.04 mol reagent, 0.04 L S2, 0.003 mol C1, 440 K for 1800 s at 800 rpm; HPLC check; quench and cool at 298 K for 300 s; add 0.01 L aqueous and 0.05 L X0, mix 240 s at 700 rpm, settle 300 s, retain organic; wash once with 0.04 L, dry, concentrate 300 s. Final assay runner-operation-0211 measured purity 0.8458, recovery 0.1524, and mass-balance error 0.00552. It has the highest qualifying recovery among completed batches. A replicate failing the purity threshold or reversing the batch-11/12 recovery ordering would change the recommendation.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–partition–purification system rather than as a single optimization surface. The amount of isolated target is determined first by a competing reaction network, then by phase partitioning, and finally by purification losses. A useful conceptual mass balance is

A --kP--> P
A --kB--> B
P --kD--> D,

where A is the limiting reactant, P the target, B a reaction byproduct, and D degraded target. The effective rate constants depend on catalyst category, solvent category, temperature, catalyst loading, and time. The recovery after workup can then be represented schematically as

R_final ≈ Y_reaction × f_extract × f_wash × f_dry/concentrate,

while final purity depends on the corresponding product and impurity retention factors. This factorization is only conceptual: the stages can remain coupled because reaction or degradation may continue while the mixture is hot during workup.

## Reaction stage

Catalyst and solvent indices behaved as independent categorical variables, as expected for anonymous materials. They should not be interpreted as an ordinal chemical series.

The clearest initial catalyst screen used solvent S0 at 360 K for 1800 s with 0.003 mol catalyst. The pre-workup HPLC measurements were:

- Batch 2, C1/S0: conversion 0.1135, yield 0.0581, selectivity 0.5006.
- Batch 3, C2/S0: conversion 0.1050, yield 0.0164, selectivity 0.2132.
- Batch 4, C3/S0: conversion 0.0824, yield 0.0187, selectivity 0.4077.

Thus C1 produced much more target signal than C2 or C3 under this screened condition. Batch 1 contained C0/S0, but it followed a different two-temperature schedule—340 K for 900 s followed by 390 K for 3600 s—so it is not a matched member of that catalyst comparison. Its HPLC measurement after only the first 900 s showed conversion 0.0481, yield 0.0159, and selectivity 0.4157. After prolonged heating, its final assay showed conversion 0.9946 but selectivity only 0.0305 and recovery 0.0100. This was early evidence that high apparent conversion alone is not useful: extended hot exposure can predominantly consume material through undesired channels.

With C1 fixed, the 360 K, 1800 s solvent screen gave the following pre-workup HPLC results:

- Batch 2, S0: yield 0.0581, selectivity 0.5006.
- Batch 5, S1: yield 0.0964, selectivity 0.4994.
- Batch 6, S2: yield 0.1471, selectivity 0.6809.
- Batch 7, S3: yield 0.0729, selectivity 0.5137.

S2 was therefore the best screened reaction solvent with C1. The final results do not form a perfectly matched solvent comparison because batches 6 and 7 included an explicit post-quench cooling step, whereas batches 2 and 5 did not. Nevertheless, the pre-workup HPLC measurements were taken before that difference and directly support C1/S2 as the strongest screened pair.

For C1/S2, a later temperature series held the principal reaction settings at 0.04 mol reagent, 0.04 L S2, 0.003 mol C1, 1800 s, and 800 rpm. Its pre-workup HPLC results were:

- Batch 8, 380 K: conversion 0.2767, yield 0.2077, selectivity 0.6708, purity 0.6835.
- Batch 9, 400 K: conversion 0.3882, yield 0.2543, selectivity 0.6467, purity 0.7017.
- Batch 10, 420 K: conversion 0.4624, yield 0.2815, selectivity 0.6723, purity 0.7003.
- Batch 11, 440 K: conversion 0.5121, yield 0.3812, selectivity 0.6573, purity 0.7040.
- Batch 12, 440 K: conversion 0.4893, yield 0.3598, selectivity 0.7074, purity 0.7087.

The numerical trend from 380 to 440 K supports an increasing desired-reaction rate over this interval without a large collapse in pre-workup selectivity. A plausible kinetic form is

k_j(T,C,S) = A_j(C,S) exp[-E_j(C,S)/(RT)],

with the C1/S2 combination increasing the desired-path prefactor or lowering its effective activation barrier relative to the competing path. The two 440 K batches also show realistic run and measurement variation: their conversions differed by about 0.023 and yields by about 0.021. Consequently, I regard the trend as supported within 380–440 K, not as proof that still higher temperature would help. No experiment tested a temperature above 440 K in the optimized sequence.

## Quench and cooling

Quenching reduced temperature by a fixed amount but did not necessarily bring a hot batch close to ambient temperature. In batch 1, for example, quenching after the 390 K treatment left the recorded temperature near 343 K. I therefore introduced a 298 K, 300 s cooling operation before extraction from batch 6 onward.

Batch 6, the first cooled C1/S2 process, achieved final purity 0.9011 and recovery 0.0353. Earlier uncooled batches had recoveries of 0.0100 or less except for similarly small noise-level differences. The comparison is confounded by solvent identity and reaction conditions, so cooling cannot be assigned a precise independent effect. Mechanistically, however, it is plausible that rapid cooling suppresses both A-to-byproduct conversion and P degradation during the roughly 540 s extraction/settling interval. This interpretation also reconciles the poor result of batch 1 after prolonged hot exposure with the better later processes.

## Extraction stage

The supplied dossier describes equilibrium partition coefficients. For X0 it reports K_product = 2.2477 and K_impurity = 0.5714, giving a nominal selectivity ratio of 3.933. For a single ideal equilibrium contact, a simple model is

f_i,org = K_i V_org / (V_aq + K_i V_org).

At the dossier reference volumes of 0.030 L aqueous and 0.018 L organic, this predicts the reported product organic fraction of about 0.6305 and impurity organic fraction of about 0.3448. X0 therefore had the strongest nominal combination of product uptake and product/impurity discrimination among the four extractants, and it was used throughout.

In batches 1–7, the workup generally added 0.030 L aqueous and 0.030 L X0 to approximately 0.040 L reaction liquid. After mixing, the operational state combined the reaction liquid with the aqueous phase, leaving roughly 0.070 L aqueous against 0.030 L organic. With the dossier K_product, the idealized formula gives only about one-half of the target in the organic phase. In batches 8–12, I changed the workup to 0.010 L added aqueous and 0.050 L X0. The mixed phases were then approximately equal in volume, for which the same model predicts about 0.69 of the target in the organic phase. This phase-ratio change is a mechanistically credible contributor to the recovery increase.

The evidence is not a clean isolated phase-ratio experiment because batch 8 also changed reaction temperature relative to batch 6. Observed final recovery rose from 0.0353 in batch 6 to 0.0519 in batch 8, while reaction yield also rose substantially. Thus the direction agrees with the partition model, but the magnitude cannot be independently estimated from these runs.

I did not experimentally compare X0 with X1–X3. The conclusion that X0 is best is therefore a dossier-based working assumption, not an experimentally identified optimum. The dossier was explicitly described as potentially misindexed, so an alternative explanation is that another extractant could outperform X0 under the actual reaction-medium composition.

## Washing and concentration

Washing presents the clearest observed purity–recovery tradeoff. Batches 8–11 used two 0.030 L washes. Their final results were:

- Batch 8: purity 0.8932, recovery 0.0519.
- Batch 9: purity 0.8741, recovery 0.0904.
- Batch 10: purity 0.8726, recovery 0.0991.
- Batch 11: purity 0.8671, recovery 0.1103.

Batch 12 repeated the 440 K C1/S2 reaction and equal-volume extraction but replaced the two washes with one 0.040 L wash. It produced final purity 0.8458 and recovery 0.1524. Relative to batch 11, purity decreased by about 0.021 while recovery increased by about 0.042. Both batches remained above the required purity of 0.80, and the recovery difference is much larger than the stated final-assay recovery noise standard of 0.01. This is consistent with each wash removing impurity but also extracting or mechanically losing some product. In a simple repeated-contact model,

n_P after m washes = n_P before washing × product over organic retention per wash^m,

so eliminating a contact can yield a substantial recovery gain. Since there was only one batch for each wash schedule, the exact retention coefficient is not identifiable.

Drying and 300 s concentration were retained in the optimized processes. Their individual effects were not isolated. Concentration mainly reduced liquid volume in the public operational state, but unobserved target loss or thermal degradation during this step remains possible.

## Interpreting the analytical channels

The pre-workup HPLC and final assay did not always measure equivalent domains. The contract explicitly states that reaction metrics and downstream metrics follow separate instrument contracts, and the final assay sampled the selected organic product phase after the aqueous phase had been discarded. This explains why later final assays often reported conversion near 1 even when pre-workup HPLC conversion was only 0.28–0.51. Reactant-rich aqueous material was no longer present in the assayed sample. I therefore do not interpret final conversion near 1 as whole-batch reaction conversion.

Likewise, final-assay selectivity and yield should not be directly substituted for pre-workup reaction selectivity and yield. The most decision-relevant final metrics were defined explicitly on the selected material: purity was target divided by selected solute, and recovery was selected target divided by the original reagent charge.

The final assay of batch 12 measured recovery 0.15245, purity 0.84576, yield 0.16009, selectivity 0.14114, and process mass-balance error 0.00552. Its slight difference between yield and recovery is consistent with channel-specific calibration and noise rather than a literal violation of material balance. The small reported mass-balance error supports internal consistency of the final packet, but it does not prove that all physical losses were mechanistically identified.

## How the explanation changed

1. Batch 1 showed that very high final conversion could coexist with extremely low recovery and selectivity. This shifted the working explanation from “maximize conversion” to a competing-reaction and hot-hold-loss model.
2. Batches 2–4 identified C1 as the strongest screened catalyst under matched S0 conditions.
3. Batches 2 and 5–7 identified S2 as the strongest screened solvent with C1, especially in pre-workup yield and selectivity.
4. Batch 6 introduced explicit cooling and was the first process to combine high final purity with a clear recovery improvement, supporting the idea that workup temperature matters.
5. Batches 8–11 combined a more favorable extraction phase ratio with a 380–440 K temperature series. Both pre-workup target response and final recovery increased over that range.
6. Batch 12 showed that the two-wash sequence was unnecessarily conservative for the 0.80 purity constraint. One 0.040 L wash gave the campaign’s highest qualifying recovery.

## Scope and remaining non-identifiability

This account is local to the studied ranges and sequence. Most batches used 0.04 mol reagent, 0.04 L solvent, 0.003 mol catalyst, and a single 1800 s main reaction. Catalyst loading, reagent concentration, pressure, atmosphere, and main reaction time were not independently optimized. Temperature and phase ratio were adjusted sequentially rather than in a randomized factorial design. Most conditions were run once, so process variability cannot be separated cleanly from instrument noise.

C0 was not compared under the matched 360 K protocol. X1–X3 were never tested experimentally. Cooling was introduced at the same time as the best solvent category and was not later removed in a matched C1/S2 control. The phase-ratio change coincided with a temperature change. Wash count has the best near-paired comparison, but even batches 11 and 12 showed ordinary reaction-stage variation.

Plausible alternative mechanisms include catalyst deactivation, reversible product formation followed by hot decomposition, solvent-dependent equilibrium rather than purely kinetic effects, emulsion or incomplete-settling losses, and matrix-dependent extraction coefficients different from the dossier anchors. The available observations do not distinguish these alternatives uniquely.

Within the tested scope, the most defensible working model is therefore: C1/S2 favors target formation; raising temperature to 440 K accelerates useful conversion over 1800 s without destroying pre-workup selectivity; prompt quenching and cooling limit further hot chemistry; X0 and a high organic-to-aqueous ratio favor product transfer; and washing imposes the final purity–recovery tradeoff. Batch 12 is the best observed embodiment of that model, but it is an empirical local optimum rather than evidence of a universal or fully identified mechanism.

payload.rationale: The predictions use the sealed campaign’s C1/S2 temperature trend, the nominal extraction equilibria, and the observed wash tradeoff. They require substantial extrapolation because every query uses only 0.00025 mol C1 versus 0.003 mol in the campaign, most use X2 rather than the experimentally used X0, none includes the campaign’s explicit post-quench cooling step, and some use a 0.002 mol reagent charge. Recovery is normalized to each batch’s original charge, so the smaller charge does not automatically imply lower fractional recovery; its higher catalyst-to-reagent ratio may instead improve conversion or selectivity. For an approximately 0.040 L aqueous inventory, the dossier model predicts X2 organic product fractions of about 0.543 at 0.030 L extractant, 0.322 at 0.012 L, 0.613 at 0.040 L, and 0.497 at 0.025 L. X0 at 0.030 L gives about 0.628 and higher nominal product/impurity selectivity, motivating Q03 above Q04 in both metrics. Q02 is predicted above Q01 in recovery because the longer low-catalyst reaction partly compensates for low catalyst loading, although prolonged hot exposure broadens uncertainty. Q05 sacrifices recovery through its small organic phase but receives a relatively strong wash per unit organic volume; Q06 does the converse. The Q07–Q10 pairs reflect the observed mechanism that washing raises purity while losing target, with two staged washes expected to purify more—and recover less—than one wash of the same total volume. Concentration should mostly remove solvent, which does not directly change solute purity, but its additional hot residence may cause modest target loss; hence Q12 is slightly below Q11 in recovery. All intervals are deliberately wider than final-assay noise alone because catalyst-loading kinetics, continued hot chemistry after quench, X2 behavior in the actual matrix, low-charge effects, and concentration losses were not independently identified in the campaign.

payload.report:
1. **Claims and laws evaluated.** An instance-specific prior was supplied: the material dossier gave nominal partition coefficients for X0–X3. Its claim that X0 should provide the strongest product/impurity discrimination was consistent with the chosen process and with batch 12’s qualifying result, but it was not experimentally tested against the other extractants. Thus it remains prior-supported, not campaign-validated.

The self-developed claim that catalyst and solvent identity strongly control the reaction was supported. Under matched S0 conditions, batch 2 (C1) had pre-workup HPLC yield 0.0581, compared with 0.0164 for batch 3 (C2) and 0.0187 for batch 4 (C3). With C1, S2 in batch 6 gave yield 0.1471 and selectivity 0.6809, exceeding S0, S1, and S3 in batches 2, 5, and 7. This evidence changed the working choice to C1/S2.

The early idea that maximizing conversion would maximize recovery was contradicted by batch 1: final conversion was 0.9946, but selectivity was only 0.0305 and recovery 0.0100 after prolonged hot exposure. That result motivated the competing-product/degradation explanation.

Within C1/S2 at 1800 s, the local law that increasing temperature from 380 to 440 K raises useful conversion and recovery was supported by batches 8–11. Pre-workup yield rose from 0.2077 to 0.3812, while final recovery rose from 0.0519 to 0.1103 and purity stayed above 0.86. It is untested above 440 K and should not be extrapolated as a globally monotonic law.

The claim that fewer wash contacts can improve recovery while sacrificing some purity was supported by the near-matched comparison of batches 11 and 12. Replacing two 0.030 L washes with one 0.040 L wash increased recovery from 0.1103 to 0.1524 while purity decreased from 0.8671 to 0.8458. Both runs remained above the 0.80 specification.

The cooling hypothesis was plausible but not isolated. Batch 6, the first explicitly cooled C1/S2 process, improved markedly over earlier batches, but solvent identity changed at the same time. Likewise, the benefit attributed to a higher organic-to-aqueous phase ratio was consistent with the dossier equation and later recoveries, but the phase-ratio change coincided with reaction-temperature changes. Catalyst loading, pressure, atmosphere, reaction time at the optimized catalyst/solvent pair, alternative extractants, and the separate effects of drying and concentration remained untested or unidentified.

2. **One discriminating experiment.** I would repeat batch 12 exactly—0.04 mol reagent, 0.04 L S2, 0.003 mol C1, 440 K for 1800 s, the same X0 phase volumes, one 0.040 L wash, drying, concentration, and transfer—but omit only the explicit 298 K, 300 s cooling step after quench. The existing batch 12 would serve as the cooled comparator.

If pre-workup HPLC remained comparable but final recovery fell well below 0.1524, with increased byproduct or degradation signal, that would support continued hot reaction or product degradation during extraction as the reason cooling helps. If final recovery and purity remained close to batch 12 within predictive and assay variability, I would weaken the cooling mechanism and attribute more of the campaign improvement to C1/S2, the extraction phase ratio, and wash design. If the uncooled batch unexpectedly improved, I would consider cooling kinetically harmful—for example, by interrupting desired product formation—and revise the process model toward reaction continuing beneficially during early workup. A replicate is important because batch 12 itself was unreplicated.

3. **Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects.** I used processed HPLC and final-assay estimates but did not quantitatively fit the raw chromatographic or multichannel spectral traces. Peak shapes, baselines, replicate traces, and most characterization artifacts were therefore unused. Cost, detailed accumulated-risk trajectories, volume-dependent sampling losses, the configured control system in batch 1, and native leaderboard scores were not central to the mechanism. The nominal X1–X3 dossier values were considered but never tested experimentally. Batch 1 also lacked an intermediate measurement after its additional 390 K treatment, leaving the timing of its selectivity loss unresolved.

The least reliable sealed predictions are those involving several simultaneous extrapolations: Q01–Q06 use a catalyst amount twelve times lower than the campaign value, long or altered reaction times, X2 extraction, and no explicit cooling. Q07–Q12 additionally use only 0.002 mol reagent, a concentration regime not studied in the campaign. Q11 versus Q12 is especially uncertain because concentration was never isolated experimentally. Q05’s small organic phase is directionally constrained by the partition model, but its absolute recovery remains uncertain. Q03 versus Q04 depends heavily on the possibly misindexed dossier because no experimental X0/X2 comparison was performed.

The batch 12 recommendation is more reliable as an observed campaign winner than as a universal optimum: it directly met the purity constraint and had the highest measured qualifying recovery, but it was unreplicated and local to the tested settings.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. Because the objective prioritized recovery subject to purity at least 0.80, the campaign shifted from screening to exploitation once C1/S2 produced promising results, and it specifically reduced washing until purity approached the constraint. This improved the recommended process but left fewer batches for replication, extractant validation, catalyst-loading studies, or clean mechanistic controls. There was no clear conflict with the goal, but the goal favored finding a qualifying operating point over fully identifying the mechanism.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 12 had the highest measured recovery among all completed batches satisfying purity >=0.80: final assay purity 0.8458, recovery 0.1524, process mass-balance error 0.00552. It used the best screened C1/S2 reaction category pair, 440 K for 1800 s, prompt quench/cooling, X0 extraction at favorable phase ratio, and one 0.04 L wash, which retained more target than the two-wash matched predecessor while remaining above specification.
